column1: # Hand-written search queries with their intended answer, for the "queries" eval mode.
# Format: <query> TAB <expected MangaBaka title> TAB <class>
# Lines starting with # are comments.
# EVERY title here was checked against the dump before being committed. That is not bureaucracy: a
# label that does not resolve scores as a miss for every model, which reads as a model failure and
# is actually a typo. Titles are MangaBaka's, which are often NOT the common English ones -
# "Detective Conan" not "Case Closed", "Omniscient Reader" without "'s Viewpoint", "Gambling
# Apocalypse Kaiji", "Saiki Kusuo no Ψ-nan". Several well-known series are absent from the
# recommendable pool entirely (Komi Can't Communicate, Watamote, Yuri!!! on Ice) and their queries
# were dropped rather than left in to score zero forever.
# A famous series usually has SEVERAL rows in the pool (Naruto 15, Sword Art Online 23, Gundam 26 -
# sequels, spin-offs, anthologies). Scoring must therefore accept ANY row whose title matches the
# label, not one chosen id: a search for "naruto" that returns "Naruto: The Seventh Hokage" has not
# failed. This does mean a query with 26 acceptable rows is easier than one with 1, so the absolute
# MRR is optimistic - but every model faces the identical bias, and the paired comparison is what
# decides anything.
# The classes are scored separately because they ask different things of the index, and one
# averaged number hides the only result that matters:
#   alias        An abbreviation or fan nickname. This is the LEXICAL channel's job - the FTS5 title
#                index and the alt-title rows. Dense retrieval measures ~0.09 MRR on short alias
#                queries and no model swap fixes that, so losing here means little on its own.
#   title        The real title, misspelled or half-remembered. Also mostly lexical, but a dense
#                model should not be actively wrong.
#   premise      A description of the story containing no title words. This is the DENSE channel's
#                job and the reason the exercise exists: the query shape a title index cannot
#                answer at all.
#   creator      A person's name, with or without an author:/artist:/studio: prefix.
#   typo         A misspelling the fuzzy rescue has to survive.
#   filtered     A `premise` query repeated with a filter set in the optional fourth column.
# Only `premise` should decide a model swap. The other classes catch a candidate that wins on
# premise by wrecking everything else.
# OPTIONAL FOURTH FIELD: filters, as `key=value;key=value`, values comma-separated for the list
# filters (genre, tag, type, status, rating) and plain for yearmin, yearmax, minrating, minchapters
# and maxchapters. Filters are their own code path - a row mask on the FilterPlan, applied per row
# BEFORE the top-K rather than to the result page, and duplicated in C# from
# RecommendationFilters.BuildClause - and nothing measured it until this column existed. Every
# filter below was checked against the dump: at least one row carrying the label satisfies it, so a
# miss is a ranking failure and not an impossible query.
